summary.case_overview: This landmark constitutional case addressed the scope and limits of the amending power under Article 368 of the Constitution of India, as well as the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 1] [Page 2]. The petitions arose primarily from challenges to land reform legislation in Kerala [Page 1] [Page 2]. The full bench of 12 judges examined whether fundamental rights could be abridged or destroyed, whether implied limitations restrict the amending power, and the correctness of the earlier decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 6].
summary.facts_of_case: Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution by His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru, challenging the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969) for violating fundamental rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act No. 25 of 1971) was passed [Page 1]. Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, which latter amendment placed the Kerala Land Reforms Acts into the Ninth Schedule [Page 2]. The petitioners amended their writ petitions to challenge these constitutional amendments [Page 2]. The matter was referred by a Constitution Bench to a larger bench [Page 2].

summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners urged that the Constitution gave Indian citizens freedoms that were to subsist forever, and that the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution is limited [Page 2]. They contended that Parliament cannot destroy the basic features or fundamental structure of the Constitution, such as secularism, democracy, and individual freedom [Page 307] [Page 338]. They argued that fundamental rights are inalienable and cannot be amended out of existence, and that constitutional amendments are subject to implied limitations [Page 21] [Page 307] [Page 338]. Conversely, the respondents (Union of India and State respondents) claimed that Parliament has absolute, limitless, and plenary power under Article 368 to amend any and every provision of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, and that there are no implied or inherent limitations on the amending power [Page 2] [Page 175] [Page 185]. They argued that the word 'amendment' permits any degree of change, variation, addition, or repeal, and that courts cannot read unexpressed restrictions into the text [Page 175] [Page 185].
summary.court_reasoning: The 12 judges delivered separate opinions containing diverse reasoning on the scope of Article 368 and the validity of the amendments. Certain judges reasoned that the amending power under Article 368 is subject to inherent or implied limitations, meaning that while provisions may be amended, the basic structure, core identity, or fundamental features of the Constitution (such as democracy, secularism, and sovereignty) cannot be destroyed or abrogated from within [Page 307] [Page 338]. Other judges reasoned that Article 368 contains a wide, comprehensive, and unambiguous power to amend every provision of the Constitution without any implied restrictions, and that the text of the Constitution permits no such judicial importation of limitations [Page 175] [Page 185]. Regarding the Twenty-fourth Amendment, views differed on whether it merely clarified or expanded pre-existing constituent power [Page 113] [Page 216]. Regarding the Twenty-fifth Amendment, contentions centered on whether substituting 'amount' for 'compensation' under Article 31(2) and barring judicial review via Article 31C violated basic principles or judicial review [Page 195] [Page 298].
